title: Gateless Barrier, Case 2: Baizhang's Fox
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk highlights the importance of understanding karma and its complexities in Buddhist teachings, particularly when it comes to enlightened beings. It emphasizes that even those who have achieved enlightenment are not completely free from cause and effect, but rather navigate it with clarity. Nomon Tim Burnett encourages listeners to consider the power of their words, thoughts, and actions, acknowledging that they can create harm or benefit, and to cultivate greater awareness and wisdom through this understanding.

One of the purposes of looking at these stories is that it introduces us to a cast of characters, the Zen family, at least the way Zen looks at its own family.
That tends to be a group of Chinese teachers from about the seventh through the tenth century, the Tang dynasty and the beginning of the Song dynasty.
I remember at one point noticing that fact and asking somebody, I don't know who: what about the thousand years after that?
Did nothing happen?
There's some stuff that's been recorded about what happened in Zen history between these characters and us, but not nearly as much.
Most traditions pick a golden age, as a mythic way to explore and celebrate something about the human heart.
So this is not exactly history so much as a certain kind of mythology based on history.
Like I mentioned before, one of the Zen scholars I like says the more important it is, probably the less historically true it was.
Last week we met the teacher Zhaozhou, an important teacher in this particular set.
Tonight we meet Bai Zhang.

The teacher also has multiple names.
Even just taking one name, the primary name is transliterated two different ways in English from the Chinese, and then the Japanese have their own way of saying it.
So here's Zhaozhou from last week.

Sounds vaguely like Zhaozhou, Zhou Zhou, Zhou Shu.
But in story two, we meet Bai Zhang.
Starts with a B or a P, depending, in Chinese.
And the Japanese mysteriously call Bai Zhang Hyaku Zhou.
Hyaku Zhou.
I'm sure there's a logic to how they got from point A to point B, but we don't know what it is.
The first story was a very short story, a question and answer exchange between a student and the teacher about Buddha nature, using the example of a dog: the famous Zhaozhou's Mu.
A student asking, either to check things out or because he was confused or who knows why, just to be thorough: so does a dog have Buddha nature?
Zhaozhou famously said, "Not."
And that has led to many millions of hours of zazen and commentary and contemplation.
Not.

"No" is like negation.
This is much more like the contemporary use of "not": wouldn't it be great to blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, not.
Story two, on the other hand, is a very long story.
So here it is.
This is the famous story of Bai Zhang's fox.
*Once when Bai Zhang gave a series of Dharma talks, a certain old man was always there listening together with the monks.
When they left, he would leave too.
One day, however, he remained behind.
And so Bai Zhang, the teacher, asked him, "Who are you, standing before me?"
The old man replied, "I'm not a human being."*
Interesting opening.
I'm not a human being.
*"In the far distant past, in the time of Kasyapa Buddha, I was the head priest on this mountain.

One day a monk asked me, 'Does an enlightened person fall under the law of cause and effect or not?' I replied, 'Such a person does not fall under the law of cause and effect.' And with this, I was reborn as a fox five hundred times."*
Five hundred lifetimes as a fox.
*"Please say a turning word for me to release me from the body of the fox."
And so the man asked Bai Zhang, the teacher, "What do you say?
Does an enlightened person fall under the law of cause and effect or not?"
Bai Zhang said, "Such a person does not evade the law of cause and effect."
Hearing this, the old man was immediately enlightened.
Making his bows, he said, "I am released from the body of the fox.
The body is on the other side of the mountain.
I wish to make a request of you.
Please, Abbot, perform my funeral as for a priest."*
*And so Bai Zhang had the head monk strike the signal board and inform the assembly that after the noon meal there would be a funeral service for a priest.
The monks talked about this in wonder.
"All of us are well.
There's nobody in the morgue.
What does the teacher mean?"
After the meal, Bai Zhang led his monks to the foot of a rock on the far side of the mountain.
And there with his staff he poked out the body of a dead fox.
He then performed the ceremony of cremation.
And that evening he took the high seat before his assembly and told his monks the whole story.
His student, Wang Bo, stepped forward and said, "As you say, the old man missed the turning word and was reborn as a fox 500 times.
What if he had given the right answer each time he was asked such a question?
What would have happened then?"
Bai Zhang said to him, "Just step up here closer and I'll tell you."
Wang Bo went up to Bai Zhang and slapped him in the face.*
Students slap the teacher, it says.
